column4: The ayah itself names a غاشية that may come from God's punishment, joining the section's arriving cover, its punitive scope, and its warning question in one formulation.
Fire تغشى the criminals' faces while their pitch garments surround their bodies; this is the section's crushing outer cover landing first on the exposed front of the person.
Dark pieces of night seem to have been أُغْشِيَتْ over the evildoers' faces; the ayah turns the section's night-as-cover into the visible mark of judgment.
The smoke يغشى الناس and is immediately identified as painful punishment, making the Ghashiya movement a palpable cover that reaches people from the sky.
Punishment يغشاهم from above them and from beneath their feet; it realizes the section's cover as total enclosure rather than a sheet resting only overhead.
Hell is a bed beneath its people and غواش above them, giving the punitive cover both a lower support and upper layers exactly as the section's enclosure requires.
The damned have canopies of fire above and canopies beneath, and God uses this scene to make His servants fear; the enclosing cover has become the thing feared.
A wave يغشاه, above it another wave, and above that a cloud, until layered darkness prevents sight; this concretely joins surrounding cover, descent from above, and blinded perception.
A wave يغشيهم like canopies, prompting sincere prayer, yet rescue is followed by denial; the ayah binds an overwhelming cover to the exposure and return of kufr.
What covered Pharaoh's people from the sea غشيهم; the deliberately repeated covering verb makes annihilating water another concrete form of the all-enveloping event.
God covered the overturned settlements with what covered them, فغشاها ما غشى; the unspecified cover conveys the same overwhelming completeness carried by the name Ghashiya.
A غشاوة lies over the disbelievers' sight after their resistance to warning; the section's claim that covering truth ends in covered perception is stated bodily here.
Barriers enclose the rejecters before and behind, then God says فأغشيناهم so they do not see; an outer enclosure becomes an inward failure of sight.
The self-deifying follower of desire has hearing and heart sealed and a غشاوة placed over sight; this shows truth-covering as a cover that reaches the faculties of understanding.
Those with diseased hearts look like one يُغشى عليه من الموت when fighting is disclosed; this is the source section's secondary sense of an event covering understanding into a faint.
Fear makes the hypocrites' eyes roll like one يُغشى عليه من الموت; an external danger reaches consciousness and overwhelms it, enacting the section's inward extension of the cover.
The oath by night when it يغشى supplies the section's explicit natural model: darkness arrives from outside and covers what had been visible.
Night is sworn by when it يغشاها, covering the sun; this repeated night image clarifies covering as the withdrawal of visibility rather than mere contact.
God makes night يغشي the day, pursuing it swiftly; the verse gives the Ghashiya root a recurrent cosmic motion in which one expanse is laid over another.
Night يغشي the day amid the ordering of earth, rivers, and fruits; the recurring cover belongs to the same created world in which garden growth can shelter the ground.
Night جنّ over Abraham and hid the field of sight; this is the second root in the section's three-root night image and makes j-n-n's concealment sensory and concrete.
The abyss is identified as نار حامية, repeating the exact fire description outside surah 88 and keeping the root's burning sense beside the section's protected-place dictionary branch.
The rain-grown crop delights the الكفار in the verse's farmer sense, then yellows and crumbles before final punishment or forgiveness; productive covering and final outcomes meet explicitly.
Believers are pictured as a crop that emerges, thickens, and delights its sowers while enraging the disbelievers; the ayah sets fruitful cultivation directly against kufr.
Dhu al-Qarnayn finds a people for whom God made no ستر against the sun; this is the section's dictionary picture of the uncovered person with no barrier toward the sky.
God makes shade, mountain shelters, and garments that protect from heat and violence; these are the creaturely covers whose presence defines by contrast what the punished person has lost.
The people of the Garden turn toward one another and ask, beginning the remembered family conversation that the section invokes before their statement of protection.
They say that formerly, among their family, they lived in fear; this supplies the precise earlier stance from which the Garden's protective cover is understood.
They say God favored them and وقانا the scorching punishment; the protecting verb is exactly the verb used in the section's dictionary definition of a shield.
They recall that they used to call upon God and name Him gracious and merciful; their former appeal completes the passage's movement from fear to bestowed protection.
No soul knows what comfort has been hidden for it as reward; this directly states the section's claim that the Garden is a recompense still covered from present perception.
The promised Gardens of Eden are بالغيب, belonging to the unseen while God's promise will arrive; hidden reward and eventual arrival are joined in one ayah.
God protects the righteous from the evil of that Day and meets them with radiance and joy; protection from the overwhelming event appears visibly on their faces.
Their patience is repaid with a Garden and silk, giving the positive cover that follows God's protection from the Day in the preceding ayah.
Reclining in the Garden, they encounter neither sun nor bitter cold; the reward removes the exposed person's direct vulnerability to the sky.
The Garden's shades hang close over them and its fruit is lowered within reach; trees form the sheltering cover that the section hears in the name jannah.
Those who believe enter gardens and are admitted into ظلا ظليلا, abundant deep shade; the Garden's reward is explicitly figured as a protective covering.
The promised Garden has lasting fruit and lasting shade, while the rejecters' end is fire; enduring tree-cover and punitive exposure are placed at the passage's boundary.
The companions of the Garden and their spouses are occupied joyfully في ظلال on couches; Paradise is staged as life beneath sheltering shade.
Extended shade is one of the concrete provisions for the companions of the right; the Garden's covering is spacious, sustaining, and non-crushing.
The God-fearing are amid shades and springs, directly answering the false fire-shadow assigned to the rejecters earlier in the same surah.
Dust lies on faces on that Day, placing a material-looking cover on the very surface the section identifies as the first place struck.
Darkness ترهق those faces, adding a second oppressive layer over the dust and closely repeating the section's night-covered face.
The dust-darkened faces are identified as those who kafarū and transgressed; the passage joins the truth-coverer to the face that has itself become covered.
Faces are humbled before the Living, Self-Sustaining Lord, and the bearer of wrongdoing fails; this directly repeats the eschatological face lowered by the event.
Their eyes are humbled and humiliation ترهقهم, covering them after they refused the summons while able; moral refusal becomes an enveloping public abasement.
They rush from the graves with lowered eyes while humiliation ترهقهم; the promised Day arrives as the cover of abasement already pictured on the faces of surah 88.
The wrongdoers are presented to the Fire خاشعين من الذل and look furtively; the section's humbled face becomes a whole posture under punishment.
Their eyes had been under a غطاء from God's reminder and they could not hear; the ayah directly joins chosen inattention to a cover over perception.
The rejecters claim their hearts are in أكنة, their ears bear heaviness, and a veil stands between them and the messenger; resistance is described as layered insulation from truth.
God places أكنة over their hearts lest they understand and heaviness in their ears, after which they turn their backs; the cover works inward upon comprehension.
Some listen while covers are placed over their hearts so they do not understand and heaviness is in their ears; sensory access remains while meaning is hidden.
At judgment the heedless person's غطاء is removed and sight becomes sharp; the earlier perceptual cover vanishes precisely when the overwhelming reality can no longer be hidden.
What people earned has rusted over their hearts; the nonlexical heart-cover shows how repeated acts can conceal truth from within before the final outer cover arrives.
After the garden's ruin, its owner has no party to help him apart from God and cannot defend himself; garden-cover and human protection disappear together.
When the people turn away, the flood of the dam replaces their two gardens with bitter, sparse growth; a sheltering productive landscape is stripped through refusal.
The exchange of gardens is called repayment for their kufr, and the verse asks whether anyone but the deeply ungrateful is so repaid; truth-covering yields a devastated cover.
A rainstorm strips the dust from a smooth rock and leaves it bare, making ostentatious giving yield nothing; the verse ends with the people who kafarū unguided.
A good word is like a good tree with a firm root and branches in the sky; truth becomes the living upward-grown cover implicit in the section's garden.
The good tree gives fruit in every season by its Lord's leave; the verse supplies what can grow from a sound planting rather than from covering truth.
An evil word is like an uprooted tree with no stability; it is the specific reversal of the section's fruitful farmer-cover, producing no enduring shelter.
The throne-bearing angels ask forgiveness for the repentant and ask God to protect them from the punishment of Hell, using protective prayer against the consuming cover.
The angels ask that the believers and their righteous families enter the promised Gardens of Eden; Garden and family are held inside the prayer for protection.
They ask God to protect them from evils, and say whoever is protected that Day has received mercy; protection is defined at the exact temporal boundary of judgment.
Believers are commanded to protect themselves and their families from a Fire fueled by people and stones; this turns remembered family fear into an urgent present duty.
God can send punishment from above or from beneath people's feet, or confound them in hostile groups; the first two possibilities anticipate the total vertical enclosure of 29:55.
Enemies come from above and below, eyes swerve, and hearts reach throats; surrounding danger penetrates sight and mind just as the section's outer cover works inward.
The command is to watch for the day when the sky brings visible smoke; this ayah supplies the descending object that covers people in the following ayah.
Before the cover closes from above and below, Hell is already said to encompass the kāfirīn; encirclement and truth-covering meet in the lead-in to 29:55.
The criminals are seen bound together in chains before pitch clothes and face-covering fire are described; their bodily enclosure begins before the fiery cover lands.
The deeds of those who kafarū are a mirage that leaves the thirsty finder with nothing; this supplies the fruitless truth-cover immediately before the layered darkness of 24:40.
The warning makes no difference to those who kafarū, and they will not believe; this identifies the resistant stance upon which the eye-cover descends in 2:7.
After distress, security is sent down as drowsiness يغشى a group; the same inwardly reaching cover that can overwhelm understanding here calms and protects it.
Drowsiness يغشيكم as security from God before purifying rain; a descending cover becomes reassurance rather than the terror carried by Ghashiya.
For those who do good, neither darkness nor humiliation covers their faces; this explicit protected face is the immediate boundary against the night-covered faces of 10:27.
The hypocrites take their oaths as جنة, a shield, to obstruct God's path, but receive humiliating punishment; a self-made verbal cover cannot provide the protection its root promises.
Their oaths are used as جنة while they turn others from God's path; the shield sense of the Garden root is exposed here as a deceptive cover for corrupt action.
A person has only his face with which to ward the evil punishment on Resurrection; the first surface struck has become a last, inadequate shield because every other cover is gone.
The rejecters cannot keep the Fire from their faces or backs and receive no help; punishment reaches exposed fronts and rears when no protective covering remains.
The companions of the left are in a shade of black smoke, turning the Garden's sheltering tree-cover into a suffocating imitation of shade.
That smoke-shade is neither cool nor generous; the ayah states exactly why this cover fails the protective work performed by Garden shade.
The rejecters are ordered toward a three-branched shadow; the command offers the outward form of shelter as part of punishment.
The three-branched shadow neither shades nor protects from flame; it is the section's shield definition negated inside a counterfeit cover.
The punishment of the Day of the Canopy seizes the deniers; a cloud-like overhead cover, normally capable of shade, becomes the named vehicle of a terrible punishment.
The mountain is raised over the people as though it were a canopy and they think it will fall; an overhead cover becomes covenantal terror rather than shelter.
God shades Israel with clouds and sends food, so the descending overhead cover gives provision and safety rather than punishment.
God again shades the tribes with clouds while providing manna, quails, and water; the repeated canopy is a life-giving cover from above.
Noah's son seeks a mountain to protect him from the water, but no protector exists from God's command and the wave intervenes; imagined shelter fails inside an overwhelming flood.
The disbelievers have punishment in this life, harsher punishment in the next, and no wāqī from God; the protective verb underlying the section's shield is explicitly denied.
On the Day of turning away, people have no protector from God; flight exposes the person for whom every sheltering relation has closed.
When the human asks where to flee on that Day, the answer is that there is no refuge; the overwhelming event removes every possible outer shelter.
People are told to answer before a day with no refuge from God arrives; the warning stance is sharpened by the announced absence of protective cover.
Clothing is sent down to cover nakedness and as adornment, while the garment of reverence is better; bodily and inward coverings are distinguished as genuine gifts.
Satan stripped the first parents of their clothing to expose what had been hidden; the verse makes loss of cover an exposure produced through deception.
A fruitful palm-and-grape garden is struck by a fiery whirlwind when its elderly owner is most vulnerable; cultivated cover, provision, and protection vanish together.
The Prophet is told that most people will not believe despite his eagerness; this supplies the resistant audience from which the warning question of 12:107 arises.
Recitation places a hidden veil between the Prophet and those who do not believe in the Hereafter; revealed truth itself marks the boundary their refusal cannot cross.
The one who turns away after reminder has covers placed over the heart and heaviness in the ears; deliberate truth-covering becomes incapacity to understand it.
The rejecters say their hearts are wrapped, while the ayah attributes their exclusion to kufr; the claimed inner cover functions as a defense against revealed truth.
Because they believed and then kafarū, their hearts were sealed so they do not understand; the act of covering truth results in a closed faculty.
Those who lied against God are seen on Resurrection with blackened faces; judgment makes the prior inward falsification visible on the face.
Some faces on that Day are gloomy, furnishing another direct facial condition under the approaching event.
Those faces expect a back-breaking calamity, so their visible gloom registers conscious anticipation of the crushing cover.
The Day when some faces whiten and others blacken ties darkened faces to disbelief after faith and to tasting punishment.
The whitened faces remain in God's mercy, forming the protected facial counterpart to the punished faces in the preceding ayah.
Two grape gardens are surrounded with palms and set around crops; the arrangement makes the etymological Garden visible as earth enclosed beneath cultivated growth.
The owner enters his garden while wronging himself and declares that it will never perish; he mistakes a created cover for permanent security.
He doubts the Hour and assumes an even better return, exposing the denial that makes his confidence in the garden spiritually barren.
His companion asks أَكَفَرْتَ in the middle of the garden dispute; kufr is named at the point where created protection is being treated as self-sufficient.
The companion warns that a reckoning may turn the garden into a barren slippery tract; tree-cover and fertile soil can be removed together.
Its water may sink beyond recovery, showing how the hidden support of the cultivated cover can be withdrawn.
The owner's fruit is encompassed and he wrings his hands over collapsed trellises; the garden that once enclosed the ground is itself enclosed by ruin.
Saba has two gardens on the right and left, provision within a good land; the ayah stages inhabited life between productive covers before the people's turning away.
The garden owners are tested as earlier owners were when they swore to harvest at dawn; a garden becomes the setting in which concealed intention is exposed.
A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while its owners sleep; punishment overtakes the protected plot from outside their awareness.
By morning the garden is like a dark, harvested tract; the living cover has become visually indistinguishable from night or barrenness.
The ruined garden episode is identified as punishment, with the Hereafter's punishment greater; loss of cultivated cover becomes a near image of final exposure.
The deeds of those who kafarū are ashes scattered by a violent wind, leaving them unable to retain anything earned; truth-covering produces no lasting growth or shelter.
God wraps night over day and day over night, using a nonlexical wrapping image for the same alternating cosmic cover heard in the section's night vocabulary.
God strips daylight from night and people are left in darkness; visibility appears as a removable layer, complementing the section's picture of night laid over the seen world.
Dense, entwined gardens are among God's provisions, making the Garden's name visually apt through foliage that covers and encloses the ground.
God teaches David the making of armor to protect people from their violence; the material coat performs the shielding work named in the section's definition of جنة.
The command to fear the Lord is grounded in the tremendous convulsion of the Hour; this supplies the creation-wide terror by which the section says Ghashiya covers its subjects.
The quake makes nursing mothers forget, pregnancies end, and people look intoxicated although they are not; an outer event has penetrated awareness and bodily control.
Fire scorches their faces until their mouths contort, giving another direct staging of punishment reaching the exposed front of the person.
God makes earth a bed and sky a structure, then sends rain and brings out fruit; an overhead cover, the ground below, and productive growth form a life-giving enclosure.
The wrongdoers are surrounded by a fire whose enclosing walls are described like a pavilion; the architectural form of shelter becomes the material of punishment.
The believers inhabit gardens, wear garments, and recline on couches, supplying the sheltering counterpart to the fire-pavilion that encloses the wrongdoers in 18:29.
The deniers demand that pieces of sky be dropped on them; their challenge supplies the overhead fall answered by the punitive canopy in 26:189.
Sincere spending is like a high garden whose yield doubles under rain; this is the fruitful cultivated cover set against the fire-struck garden in the following ayah.
The rejecters' spending is likened to an icy wind that strikes and destroys a people's crop; their moral covering yields a visibly ruined planting.
The faithful prayer asks for good in both lives and protection from the punishment of Fire, repeating the section's protective stance in a compact supplication.
Those reflecting on creation ask their Lord to protect them from the punishment of Fire; cosmic perception culminates in the same request for a true shield.
The God-fearing are in gardens and bliss immediately before their protection from Hell is named, making the positive cover the setting of their rescue.
The Garden people rejoice because their Lord protected them from the punishment of the Blaze; it is a second direct formulation of the protective claim later voiced in 52:27.
The Garden people taste no further death and God protects them from the punishment of Hell; hidden reward and deliverance from the crushing cover coincide.
After their deeds rust over their hearts, they are veiled from their Lord on that Day; the inward cover of 83:14 reaches its final relational consequence.
God makes the sky a protected roof, yet people turn from its signs; the normal overhead expanse is a preserved shelter rather than the descending punitive cover.
God restrains the sky from falling upon earth except by His permission; the verse identifies divine mercy in holding the overhead cover safely in place.
A wall with a gate separates mercy on its inner side from punishment outside; one structure becomes the exact boundary between protective enclosure and punitive exposure.
Even if the deniers saw a piece of sky falling, they would call it a massed cloud; what appears capable of shade conceals the punishment they refuse to recognize.
God did not institute the protected livestock called hām, but disbelievers fabricated the rule; the related h-m-y protection term exposes a human-made sanctuary joined to kufr.
Faces are turned about in the Fire while their owners regret disobedience; the exposed front of the person remains the visible site on which punishment works.
When the promised punishment draws near, the faces of those who kafarū become distressed; the truth-coverer's face registers the arrival of what had been denied.
After the garden owner proves unable to protect himself, the passage says all protective authority belongs to God; this identifies the source of the only cover that endures.
The chastened garden owners hope their Lord will replace the lost plot with a better one; ruined cover becomes an occasion to seek a newly bestowed garden.
Neither wealth nor children avail those who kafarū against God, and they belong to the Fire; this identifies the people whose cultivated wealth is destroyed in the next ayah's comparison.
Their hearts are sealed because of covenant-breaking and kufr, so belief scarcely enters; covering truth is again answered by a closed faculty.
Those who prefer the nearer life over the Hereafter are identified as disbelievers whom God does not guide, establishing the choice behind the sealing described next.
God seals their hearts, hearing, and sight, leaving them heedless; the prior preference and kufr become a cover over every receiving faculty.
God extends the shadow and appoints the sun as its guide; the relation between overhead light and sheltering cover is presented as a deliberately governed sign.
God gradually draws the shadow back, making protective cover visibly removable rather than self-sustaining.
The Garden is brought near to the God-fearing after having been an unseen promise; what was covered from present perception becomes immediate.
The promised Garden belongs to one who feared the Merciful in the unseen and came with a returning heart; hidden reward answers hidden fear.
The warning asks whether people await God's decisive coming amid canopies of cloud; an overhead covering accompanies the arrival of settled judgment.
Shackles reach the rejecters' chins and constrain their heads immediately before barriers and covered sight are described; bodily enclosure precedes perceptual enclosure.
The two promised gardens possess spreading branches, giving a concise visual form to the tree-grown cover heard in the name jannah.
Those who disbelieve are asked to consider earth below and sky above, either of which could become punishment; their apparently stable enclosure depends wholly on God.
The arrival of the greatest overwhelming calamity supplies a close nonlexical name for the all-surpassing event that Ghashiya makes perceptible as a cover.
The verb تغشاها euphemistically describes one spouse covering the other before pregnancy begins; this may illuminate a life-producing bodily use of the root beside Ghashiya's destructive cover.
